chapters.title: The Translator Robot
chapters.scope: Start from zero. A program is a list of instructions; source code (text people write) vs machine code (what the CPU runs); a compiler translates the whole program ahead of time into an executable, unlike an interpreter that runs it line by line; Rust is a compiled language, so there is compile time (the compiler checks and translates) and run time (the executable runs). Classic wrong idea: a program that compiles must be correct (it can still panic at run time). What 'safe' and 'fast' mean for Rust, where Rust is used, and that Rust has editions (this book uses edition 2024). The toolbox: rustup (installer and version manager), rustc (the compiler), cargo (the build tool that calls rustc for you); install commands (`curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh` on macOS/Linux, rustup-init.exe on Windows), `rustup update`, `rustc --version`, `cargo --version`, the stable channel, components clippy/rustfmt/rust-analyzer (`rustup component add ...`), offline docs (`rustup doc --book`), the Playground as a zero-install option (it may run a different version than this book). Install pitfalls: shell not restarted so `cargo: command not found`; on Windows missing C++ build tools gives `error: linker 'link.exe' not found` (TRPL wording, not captured; say so). First program: `cargo new hello`, the folder layout (Cargo.toml = cast list, src/main.rs = script, target/ = backstage, Cargo.lock), `fn main() { }` as the starting point, braces, `println!` (the `!` means it is a macro), a string literal in double quotes, the semicolon ending a statement, comments `//` and `/* */`. `cargo run` shows Compiling / Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] / Running lines (these go to stderr, the program's text to stdout; a rerun with no change skips Compiling), `cargo build` (executable lands in target/debug), `cargo build --release` (target/release), `cargo check` (checks without producing an executable, fastest). Why `rustc main.rs` alone is a trap: it compiles as edition 2015 (`async fn` is not permitted in Rust 2015), so this book always uses cargo. First error, read slowly: a missing semicolon between two statements gives `error: expected one of '.', ';', '?', 'else', or an operator, found ...` with an arrow and caret at the spot; forgetting the `!` on println gives a real error too (capture it); read the first line (what), then the `-->` file:line:col (where), then the caret (exactly where); cargo ends with `error: could not compile` and the build exits with code 101. Catchphrase idea: the compiler is a translator robot that refuses dangerous recipes.

Variables, mut, types, numbers, {} placeholders and formatting belong to chapters 2-3; keep code to fixed println! lines (if the semicolon demo needs a `let`, keep it unexplained).

chapters.title: Red Pens and Boxes
chapters.scope: Reading the compiler as a skill (no other curriculum teaches it). Anatomy of a real error: `error[E0xxx]:` code and message, ` --> src/main.rs:L:C`, the `|` gutter with line numbers, `^^^` under the primary span with its label, `---` under secondary spans with labels (where the trouble started), `help:` blocks that show the fix with `+++` markers, `note:` lines, the closing `error: aborting due to 1 previous error` and ``For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0384`.``; cargo adds `error: could not compile ... due to 1 previous error`. Warnings vs errors (warnings still build and still appear in output); fix the first error first because later ones are often echoes; `--error-format=short` one-line form; `rustc --explain` for the long story; editor setup with VS Code + rust-analyzer (inline errors, type hints) and rustfmt on save. Classic mistakes: panicking at a wall of red, editing the line the arrow points to when the cause is the secondary label, ignoring a help: line that contains the fix. Variables: `let` makes a name for a value, immutable by default, declaration vs assignment, `let mut` to allow change; assigning twice gives `error[E0384]: cannot assign twice to immutable variable 'x'` (read it with the new anatomy: primary label, the first-assignment label, the help: suggesting `mut`). Shadowing: a second `let` with the same name makes a new variable and can change type (`let spaces = "   "; let spaces = spaces.len();`), whereas trying the same with `mut` gives `error[E0308]: mismatched types: expected '&str', found 'usize'` (just 'text type' vs 'whole-number type' for now). Type annotation `let x: i32 = 5;`. `const` (type required, SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE, value fixed at compile time); `static` mentioned only. Naming rules and snake_case; `gen` is a reserved keyword in edition 2024 (`let gen = 1;` fails with `expected identifier, found reserved keyword 'gen'`). Warnings `warning: unused variable: 'x'` and `warning: variable does not need to be mutable`, and the `_` prefix to say 'unused on purpose'. Catchphrase idea: read the red from the top, then follow the arrows.
chapters.not_yet: Number types beyond 'i32 is a whole number' and all arithmetic (chapter 3); format specs beyond `{}` and inline `{x}` (chapter 3); E0382 and ownership (chapter 7); functions (chapter 4). Use E0384 and E0308 as the worked anatomy examples, not borrow errors.

Labelled boxes: `let` is a sealed box with a window, `let mut` has a lid; shadowing is a new box with the same label placed in front of the old one (memory tracer: name tag moves to the new box, old box fades). Machine for `let`/assignment that jams with E0384. Trace exercise: label each part of a captured error; choice: shadow or mut?

chapters.title: Odometers and Speech Bubbles
chapters.scope: Number types: signed i8, i16, i32, i64, i128 and unsigned u8..u128, isize/usize (pointer-sized, used for indexes and lengths), defaults i32 and f64, floats f32/f64; literals `1_000`, `0xff`, `0b1010`, byte literal `b'a'`, suffixes like `5u8`; bool (true/false); char (single quotes, any Unicode scalar, 4 bytes). Arithmetic `+ - * / %`; integer division truncates (`7 / 2` is 3, `7 % 2` is 1) while `7.0 / 2.0` is 3.5; comparison operators produce bool; no mixing types: `3_i32 * 2.5_f64` gives `error[E0277]: cannot multiply 'i32' by 'f64'`; `as` casting basics to convert on purpose; `let c: char = "a";` gives `error[E0308]: mismatched types: expected 'char', found '&str'` (double quotes make text, single quotes make a char); `let x: u8 = 300;` gives `error: literal out of range for 'u8'`. Overflow: at run time a u8 past 255 panics with `attempt to add with overflow` in a debug build (`cargo run`) but silently wraps in a release build (`cargo run --release` printed 2 in testing), so every panel must say which profile it used; integer `/ 0` panics with `attempt to divide by zero`; the explicit methods `checked_add` (returns a maybe-value, shown just as Some/None for now), `wrapping_add`, `saturating_add`. Floats are surprising but deterministic: `0.1 + 0.2` prints `0.30000000000000004`; `1.0_f64` prints `1` with `{}` and `1.0` with `{:?}`. Printing: `println!`, `print!` (no newline), `eprintln!` (to stderr), `format!` (makes text instead of printing), `{}` Display (polite public voice) vs `{:?}` Debug (programmer X-ray), `{:#?}` pretty Debug, inline args `{x}` (Rust 1.58+, older tutorials use positional), positional `{0}`, width/alignment/padding `{:>5}` `{:<5}` `{:^5}` `{:05}`, precision `{:.2}`, escaping braces with `{{ }}`, `dbg!` (prints file:line and the expression to stderr and returns the value). A value with no Display, e.g. a tiny tuple `(3, 4)`, printed with `{}` gives `error[E0277]: ... doesn't implement 'std::fmt::Display'` while `{:?}` works (structs and `#[derive(Debug)]` come later). Classic mistakes: choosing the wrong type for age/temperature/balance, mixing types, expecting `7 / 2` to be 3.5.

chapters.title: Machines and Switches
chapters.scope: Functions: `fn name(param: Type) -> ReturnType { ... }`, every parameter needs a type (missing one is a compile error; capture it), snake_case names, calling a function and the order things run, the unit type `()` when nothing is returned, statements (do something, end in `;`) vs expressions (produce a value), a block `{ ... }` is an expression whose value is its last line without a semicolon (tail expression), `return` for leaving early, variables declared inside a block are gone after its closing brace (using one outside gives `error[E0425]: cannot find value ... in this scope`), `todo!()` as a placeholder that panics if reached. Classic mistake: a semicolon on the last line turns the value into `()` and gives `error[E0308]: mismatched types: expected 'i32', found '()'` (read the help: that suggests removing the semicolon). Informal `assert_eq!(add(2, 3), 5);` checks start here (the formal test chapter is 14). Decisions: `if`, `else if`, `else`; the condition must be a bool, Rust has no truthiness (`if n { }` with an integer gives `error[E0308]: mismatched types: expected 'bool', found integer`); `if` is an expression so `let x = if cond { 1 } else { 2 };`, and both arms must have the same type (`error[E0308]: 'if' and 'else' have incompatible types`); comparison `== != < > <= >=`, logical `&&`, the or-operator `||`, not `!`, short-circuiting (the right side is skipped when the left decides); ordering conditions in an else-if ladder (a grading ladder checked top to bottom).

chapters.title: The Guessing Game
chapters.scope: First real program, built step by step like TRPL's guessing game. `use std::io;` and `use std::cmp::Ordering;` bring names in; `let mut guess = String::new();` makes an empty growable text; `std::io::stdin().read_line(&mut guess)` reads a line into it (`&mut` is a ritual for now: 'lend it so it can be filled', explained in chapter 8); `.expect("msg")` crashes with your message if reading fails; the input arrives with a newline (the envelope edge) so `.trim()` removes it; `.parse::<u32>()` or `let guess: u32 = guess.trim().parse()...` reads the number written inside; `let n: i32 = "42".parse();` gives `error[E0308]: mismatched types: expected 'i32', found 'Result<_, _>'` because parsing might fail (Result previewed as 'a parcel that is either Ok or Err'); forgetting `.trim()` or typing `abc` with `.expect("need a number")` panics with `need a number: ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit }`; handling bad input without crashing by matching `Ok(num) => num, Err(_) => continue`. External crates: `cargo add rand` (built into cargo since 1.62; older guides edit Cargo.toml by hand), the dependency line it writes in Cargo.toml, crates.io, Cargo.lock pinning exact versions, the first build downloading crates. Comparing with `guess.cmp(&secret)` and `match` on `Ordering::Less / Greater / Equal` (match previewed, taught fully in chapter 11), wrapping it all in `loop` with `break` on a win. One-panel promise: if the compiler says expected `String`, found `&str`, call `.to_string()` for now; chapter 12 explains the two text types.

chapters.title: Plate Stacks, House Keys
chapters.scope: Memory pictures first (most curricula skip this for beginners): memory as numbered cells; the stack holds each function call's frame and works last-in-first-out (push on call, pop on return); sizes on the stack must be known at compile time; the heap holds data that can grow; a pointer is an address; a `String` is a small (pointer, length, capacity) record on the stack plus its bytes on the heap; heap access is slower (follow the ticket, find the coat); `Box::new(5)` as a first heap value. Classic wrong ideas: a String variable 'contains' its text directly; copying a variable copies its heap data. Ownership: the three rules (each value has one owner; one owner at a time; the value is dropped when its owner leaves scope); scope and the drop at the closing brace (no garbage collector, no double free, why); move on assignment `let s2 = s1;` then using s1 gives `error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: 's1'` with the label 'value moved here' and `help: consider cloning the value` (read like a detective: the cause is the secondary label); move into a function call and returning ownership back out; reusing a vector after `for x in v` consumed it (E0382, the loop preview from chapter 5); Copy types (integers, floats, bool, char, tuples of Copy types) are copied instead of moved; `.clone()` makes a deep copy of the heap data and costs time; partial moves (mention only). Catchphrase idea: one key, one owner.

chapters.title: The Library Ledger
chapters.scope: References and borrowing: `&T` is a shared reference (look, do not take), `&mut T` a mutable reference (change, still do not take); borrowing for function parameters `fn len(s: &String)` so the caller keeps ownership; references never own and never dangle; the rule: many readers OR exactly one writer at any moment; borrows end at their last use (non-lexical lifetimes), not at the closing brace; dereference with `*` to reach the value behind a reference (`*x += 1`), auto-deref when calling methods with `.`; `&mut` requires the owner to be `let mut`; finally the meaning of the `&mut guess` ritual from chapter 6. The permission model (from the Brown edition): each place has Read, Write and Own permissions; borrowing temporarily removes some of them from the owner and gives them back when the borrow ends. Real errors read like a detective: two `&mut` at once gives `error[E0499]: cannot borrow 's' as mutable more than once at a time`; pushing while holding `&v[0]` gives `error[E0502]: cannot borrow 'v' as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable`; changing through a shared reference gives `error[E0596]: cannot borrow '*s' as mutable, as it is behind a '&' reference`; a reference that outlives its value gives `error[E0597]: 'x' does not live long enough`. Teach 'a reference cannot outlive its owner' as plain words, without lifetime syntax. Catchphrase idea: many readers or one writer.

chapters.title: Case Files and Windows
chapters.scope: Fixing borrow-checker errors as a casebook (the Brown edition's best idea, absent from TRPL), one case file per error with scene (primary label), suspect (secondary label) and known fixes. Strategy list: read the secondary label first; shorten the borrow (finish using the reference before mutating); clone deliberately when you really need a second copy; take `&` instead of ownership in function parameters; return owned values instead of references; use indices instead of held references; use `Vec::remove` or `swap` to take things out; split borrows of different fields; when the checker is over-cautious, a safe library helper like `split_at_mut`. Cases: returning a reference to a local gives `error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier` (fix: return the owned value); moving out of a vector by index gives `error[E0507]: cannot move out of index of 'Vec<String>'` (fix: borrow, clone, or remove); holding a reference across `push` gives E0502 (fix: shorten the borrow or use an index); plus choose-the-best-fix exercises among three options. Slices: a slice is a view into a sequence (pointer + length) that borrows, not owns; `&s[0..5]`, shorthands `[..3]`, `[2..]`, `[..]`; array and vector slices `&[i32]`; string literals are `&'static str` (just 'text baked into the program' for now); why functions should take `&str` (works for literals and Strings); a slice keeps its owner borrowed, so clearing a String while a slice exists gives E0502; slicing in the middle of a multibyte character panics at run time with `end byte index 2 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 1..3 of string)`. Catchphrase idea: follow the suspect, not the scene.

chapters.scope: Enums: defining an enum, variants with no data, tuple-like data (`Move(i32, i32)`), struct-like data (`Write { text: String }`), methods on enums via impl. `match`: one arm per pattern, arms are expressions, exhaustiveness (a missing variant gives `error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: 'Coin::Dime' not covered`), the `_` wildcard, binding values out of a variant in a pattern, matching on Ordering (paying off chapter 6). `Option<T>`: `Some(value)` or `None` replaces null; you cannot use an Option as the value inside (`error[E0369]: cannot add '{integer}' to 'Option<&{integer}>'`); `if let Some(x) = ...`; `let ... else` (Rust 1.65+); `matches!`; `unwrap` is dangerous: `called 'Option::unwrap()' on a 'None' value` panic. chapters.title: Notebooks and Photocopies
chapters.scope: Strings in depth, paying off the chapter 6 promise. `String` is owned and growable; `&str` is a borrowed view of text; making Strings with `String::from`, `.to_string()`, `.to_owned()`, `String::new()`; growing with `push_str` (takes &str) and `push` (takes a char); `+` takes ownership of the left String and borrows the right (`s1 + &s2`; `s + String::from("b")` gives `error[E0308]: expected '&str', found 'String'`); `format!` for joining without moving anything. Text is UTF-8: `len()` counts bytes not letters (`"héllo".len()` is 6), so there is no integer indexing (`s[0]` gives `error[E0277]: the type 'str' cannot be indexed by '{integer}'` with the note that string indices are ranges of usize); walking text with `.chars()`, `.bytes()`, `.char_indices()`; slicing only on char boundaries (the chapter 9 panic revisited); common methods `trim`, `split`, `split_whitespace`, `lines`, `to_uppercase`, `replace`, `contains`, `starts_with`, `parse`; deref coercion turns `&String` into `&str` automatically; the parameter idiom: take `&str`, return `String`; passing a literal where a String is expected gives `error[E0308]: mismatched types: expected 'String', found '&str'` with `help: try using a conversion method: .to_string()`; escapes (`\n`, `\t`, `\"`, `\u{...}`) and raw strings `r"..."`. chapters.title: Lockers and Parcels
chapters.scope: Hash maps: `use std::collections::HashMap;`, `HashMap::new`, `insert` (overwrites and returns the old value as an Option), `get` returns `Option<&V>` (using it as a plain value is a classic mistake), `contains_key`, `remove`, iterating key/value pairs, inserting String keys moves them into the map, `entry(k).or_insert(v)`, counting words with `*map.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1`, `HashSet` basics (no duplicates, contains). Iteration order is unpredictable: the same 5-key map printed in three different orders across three runs; use `BTreeMap` when order matters (preview) or sort before printing. A key type without Hash/Eq gives `error[E0277]: the trait bound 'K: Eq' is not satisfied` / `'K: Hash'` (fix: derive them; traits explained later). Error handling I: panics are for unrecoverable bugs (`panic!`, exit code 101, `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` for a backtrace); `Result<T, E>` with `Ok`/`Err` for expected failures; matching a Result; `unwrap` vs `expect` and when they are acceptable (examples, tests, prototypes); `?` to pass an error up to the caller; `?` only works in functions returning Result or Option, so using it in a plain `main` gives `` error[E0277]: the `?` operator can only be used in a function that returns `Result` or `Option` `` (fix: `fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>`, Box<dyn Error> as 'any error' for now); `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_default`, `if let Err(e) = ...`; ignoring a Result gives `` warning: unused `Result` that must be used `` (#[must_use]); `.expect` failure prints `need a number: ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit }`; choosing panic vs Result for everyday scenarios.

chapters.title: Open the Restaurant
chapters.scope: Intermediate capstone: a multithreaded web server built in stages, as in TRPL's final project. A single-threaded TCP server with `std::net::TcpListener::bind` and `incoming()`, reading the request line with a BufReader, parsing it and returning an HTTP response with a status line, headers and body (including a 404); a slow route that shows why one thread blocks everyone; a thread pool with a fixed number of workers fed by a channel, with the receiver shared as `Arc<Mutex<mpsc::Receiver<Job>>>` and jobs as `Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>`; graceful shutdown by implementing `Drop` for the pool (drop the sender, then join each worker); classic mistakes: holding the lock across a long operation (it serializes the workers), forgetting to join threads on shutdown. Optional variant: the same server on Tokio. Recap every intermediate catchphrase.
chapters.not_yet: Anything beyond intermediate (async internals, unsafe, production frameworks like Axum); TLS and real HTTP libraries.
